description: Small Team working on Flame in Freefall
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive website that turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion research into fire safety insights for crewed missions on the ISS, the Moon and Mars.

Fire behaves differently in space: without gravity, hot gas doesn't rise, so flames turn round, depend on cabin airflow for oxygen, and can hide from smoke detectors. Past fires on Apollo 1 and Mir show how dangerous this is, yet future Moon and Mars habitats may use 34% oxygen air at gravity levels where almost no fire tests exist.

We built the Flame Lab, where users pick a world, set the cabin air and airflow, and see how a flame behaves. We also built a Gaps map that shows in red what NASA has never tested, ranked insights with a "How sure are we?" meter, and an AI assistant that answers only from verified findings.

Everything is built on 20 NASA experiments and sources, 39 hand-verified findings and 276 ISS fire tests. Every claim cites its NASA source. This helps mission planners and the public understand fire risk and see exactly where more research is needed.
details:
What it does

Flame in Freefall is an interactive website that turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion research into fire safety insights for crewed missions on the ISS, the Moon and Mars. It has five parts:

- Flame Lab: pick a world (ISS, Moon, Mars or Earth), set the cabin air and airflow, and see how a flame behaves there, next to what NASA actually measured in those conditions.

- Gaps map: every combination of gravity and cabin air, showing which ones NASA has tested and which have never been tested (shown in red).

- Ranked insights: fire safety lessons ordered by risk. Each has a "How sure are we?" meter that rates the evidence behind it: how many findings, how many experiments, and whether it was tested at that mission's gravity and air.

- Formulas: three NASA formulas, explained in plain words. They are computed only inside the range NASA tested; outside it, the site says "outside tested conditions" instead of guessing.

- AI assistant: answers questions using only verified NASA findings and cites the source for every claim. If the evidence doesn't exist, it says so.

How it works

We collected 20 NASA experiments and source documents and extracted 39 findings. Each one was checked by a teammate against the original paper, with the page number. We also added the full FLEX table of 276 fuel-droplet fire tests run on the ISS. All data is checked automatically on every build, so a finding without a source can't get into the site.

Benefits and impact

Fires have already endangered crews (Apollo 1 in 1967, Mir in 1997). Future Moon and Mars habitats may use 34% oxygen air at partial gravity, conditions where almost no fire tests exist. Our site helps mission planners, students and the public understand how fire behaves in space. Just as importantly, it shows where the evidence runs out, so researchers can see which experiments are needed next.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, React, Next.js, Node.js, Tailwind CSS, WebGL (for the flame visual), Zod (data validation), Vitest (automatic tests), Git and GitHub, and Vercel (hosting). The live AI chat uses free models from Groq and Google Gemini. We used Claude Code to help build the site and draft the insights, which we then reviewed by hand. NASA sources: NTRS (the technical report archive and its API), NSSDC planetary fact sheets, the NASA Image and Video Library, and the FLEX technical report (NASA/TP-2015-216046). No hardware was needed.

How it is creative

Instead of a list of papers, we let people "play" with fire in space and see the science respond. The confidence meter and the red "never tested" warnings make the gaps in knowledge visible, which most summaries hide.

Factors we considered

- Honesty: every claim cites a NASA source, and unverified data is labelled, never hidden.

- Safety of the science: formulas are computed only within their tested range.

- Accessibility: plain language, works on phones, tablets and laptops.

- Cost and reliability: free tools, no accounts and no database. If the AI is unavailable, prepared answers keep the site working during a demo.
